idiom_name: hand-written one-line method; embedded fields promote whole method sets
implementation_notes: Go gives both halves of the pattern: an embedded field promotes the embedded type's whole method set with no forwarding code at all (the language's own replacement for the classic delegating method), and when the promoted name is wrong or the exposed surface must be narrowed, an ordinary one-line method names the operation for callers - func (s OrderService) Cancel(id OrderID) error { return s.repo.Cancel(id) }. Interfaces are satisfied structurally, so the one-liner is written only where it earns a name; it is also the only way to adapt a signature or a receiver, which embedding cannot do.
pitfalls: Embedding publishes the entire method set and can satisfy interfaces you never intended; when the API must stay narrow, hand-write the one or two methods you mean instead of embedding.
A promoted call through a nil embedded pointer panics, where a hand-written wrapper could check and return an error - the one-liner is also the place to add that guard.
Receiver choices interact with embedding: adding a value-receiver method to T while the embedded field is *U silently changes which method set a T value satisfies.
